lxc_5f36284cac55ebd5.text:
Cologne and Düsseldorf love to tease each other. Beer shows it best: Kölsch is light, and Alt is dark. In a Cologne brewery pub, you never order an Alt. Alt belongs to Düsseldorf. The Cologne brewery Früh once had adverts with the slogan Not a bit of Alt. The funny part is that an agency from Düsseldorf wrote them.

The usual story says the fight started in 1288. In that year, the Archbishop of Cologne was beaten at the Battle of Worringen. On 14 August 1288, Düsseldorf received its town rights. The story says this was a thank-you for beating Cologne. Historians say this is a legend, an old story that is not true. People from both towns fought on the same side. The town rights had strategic reasons.

The real competition is newer. In 1815 both cities became part of Prussia. In the 19th century, Düsseldorf grew fast with industry. In 1946 the British chose Düsseldorf as the capital of the new state of North Rhine-Westphalia. But Cologne was much older. There were two reasons. About 90 percent of Cologne's city centre was destroyed in the war. And Düsseldorf was close to the factories of the Ruhr.

Today the rivalry lives on at carnival, the big street party before Lent. Lent is the time of the year just before Easter. In Cologne people shout Alaaf, and in Düsseldorf they shout Helau. The rivalry lives on in sport too. In football, 1. FC Köln plays against Fortuna Düsseldorf. In ice hockey, Kölner Haie play against Düsseldorfer EG. Most of it is friendly fun. In 2005 a Cologne guidebook about Düsseldorf had only empty pages. The joke was that there is nothing to see there. Cologne Zoo invited people from Düsseldorf to come and see the Cologne monkeys.
